C0.quote: properties of voting rules, i.e., of rules for selecting an outcome
C0.note: Main object is justifying the outcome of voting rules (irresolute rules on preference profiles) via axioms and computing such justifications.

C1.quote: Second, we operationalise our definition as an algorithm
C1.note: Threefold contribution: (OT) conceptual definition of justification (Def. 1, Theorem 1); (AL) encoding as constraint network and MUS-based algorithm with correctness proof (Theorem 2) and implementation; (SI) exhaustive computational experiment over all 216 synthetic profiles with 3 agents/3 alternatives; AX for results on which axioms justify which outcomes and that Black's rule satisfies all seven axioms. Primary chosen as AL since the title and Section 3 centre on automated computation; OT is a close alternative.

C2.3.note: Agents are said to have subjective preferences; the same object is also called 'declared' and 'reported' preferences.

C2.4.quote: to model the preferences of individual agents
C2.4.note: The input is the preference profile ('elements of L(X) to model the preferences of individual agents') and the rule is applied to it directly; the paper uses the words 'declared', 'reported' and 'ballots' but never states whether what is declared equals or may differ from the held preferences, so no code fits exactly; IDU chosen as closest.

VOT.note: The profile is taken as given (exogenous); agents' actions are not modelled. 'Declaring'/'reporting' language appears but no choice of report is modelled.

CAN.note: Alternatives are not modelled as agents.

ORG.note: An election committee appears only in motivating Example 1 (and its use of justifications is discussed in Section 2.2) but is not part of the formal model.

DES.note: Example 3 describes faculty choosing a decision method, but the designer's choice or objective is not modelled.

OTH.note: The 'audience' whose norms the axioms reflect is referred to but takes no modelled action.
